summary: >-
  The design takes eight signed 8-bit activations and eight signed 8-bit weights, a signed 32-bit bias, an unsigned
  16-bit multiplier, a 5-bit shift and a relu bit, all loaded through registers. A write to GO runs a pipelined
  computation: acc is the sum of the eight products plus bias, the scaled value is acc times mult divided by two to the
  power shift (rounded to nearest, exact halves towards plus infinity), and y is that value clamped to -128..127, or to
  0..127 when relu is set. The registers are reached through the UART test shell at 115200 baud (shell/PROTOCOL.md
  version 1.0). LED0 shows the READY flag. The design uses one clock, CLK100MHZ, and a synchronous reset derived from
  CPU_RESETN.
  The run got as far as RTL and the first verification stages. The Clarifier's specification was signed off and board and
  device planning passed. The RTL stage did not pass its gates. Simulation evidence reached V2 but the run asked for V3,
  and five cover properties were never hit. The run stopped because stage 2 had been visited too often. Constraints,
  synthesis, implementation, timing, power, DRC and bring-up were not run. The only Vivado build (stages rtl and
  post_synth) used an earlier release than 2026.1. The design has no measured resources, timing, power or latency.
scope_not:
- Not a general matrix or convolution engine. It computes one eight-element dot product per GO and nothing else.
- Not safe against operand writes while a result is being computed. The run assumed this is not required.
- Not defined for shift outside 1..31, for weights of -128, or for an acc that overflows 32 bits. None of these is tested.
- Not a clock-domain-crossing design. There is a single clock, and no MMCM or PLL is used.
- Not proven on hardware. No bring-up result exists.

- about: design_id_parameter
  text: >-
    spec.yaml lists DESIGN_ID as a parameter. In c14_int8_dot_requant_top.sv it is a localparam of 32'h444F5451 and
    cannot be overridden. Only CLKS_PER_BIT, TIMEOUT_CYCLES and BUILD_STAMP are top-level parameters, which matches

- about: reset_sync_source
  text: >-
    rtl/reset_sync.sv in this design is an intentionally empty file with a comment. The reset synchroniser actually
    used is shell/rtl/reset_sync.sv, which this run did not review. ARCHITECTURE.md calls it a 2-flop synchroniser, but
    the RTL here does not show it. The spec's promise that outputs clear within 2 cycles of CPU_RESETN asserting was
    not measured.
- about: reset_values
  text: >-
    After reset every operand register, bias and mult read 0, CTRL reads 1 (shift 1, relu 0), READY and the GO pulse
    are 0, and the core's y and acc registers are 0. The reset is synchronous and active high inside the design. The
    pipeline data registers in dotq_core (products, sums, and so on) are not reset, only the valid bits.
- about: unmapped_and_ro_access
  text: >-
    In dotq_regs.sv a read of any offset without a case arm returns 0. This covers 0x07 (GO), 0x0B and above, and the
    unused offsets. A write to an unmapped offset or to an RO register (Y, ACC, STATUS) is ignored by the default arm.
    This matches the spec.
- about: partial_writes_and_bit_masks
  text: >-
    Writes are whole 32-bit words with no byte strobes. MULT keeps only wdata[15:0]. CTRL keeps wdata[4:0] as shift and
    wdata[8] as relu and drops the other bits, which read back 0. Reads of MULT bits [31:16] return 0. The write data
    of a GO write is ignored. The shift field is not range-checked, so shift 0 can be stored. With shift 0 the core
    adds no rounding term and passes acc*mult through. Shift 0 is out of contract and untested.
- about: read_side_effects
  text: >-
    Reads have no side effects. The read-data register changes only on a shell read strobe and otherwise holds its
    value. Y and ACC read 0 while READY is 0 because the read is gated by ready in dotq_regs.sv. The core's own y and
    acc registers are not cleared by GO. They are overwritten when the next result is valid.
- about: go_priority_and_restart
  text: >-
    A GO write clears READY and is registered into a one-cycle go pulse to the core. If READY is being set by done in
    the same cycle as the GO write, the GO write wins and READY is 0. Inside the core a go pulse clears the valid bits
    of results in flight, so a GO while a computation is running restarts it with the loaded operands. A GO is also
    accepted when READY is already set.
- about: go_done_race
  text: >-
    Reading dotq_regs.sv and dotq_core.sv, a done pulse can reach dotq_regs in the same cycle as the registered go
    pulse, if a GO write lands one cycle before done. READY would then be set again, with the old y and acc, until the
    new done arrives. The run did not test or simulate this case. It could break the spec's rule that READY is set only
    when y and acc are valid for the latest GO. The shell's UART access time makes it unlikely in practice.
- about: latency_structure
  text: >-
    READY follows the registered go pulse through a fixed chain of valid bits in dotq_core (one per pipeline stage),
    then a registered done, then the READY flag. The spec promises READY within 8 clocks of GO. The run did not
    measure this, and it is not counted from the shell write strobe, which adds one clock for the registered go pulse.
    Only the Verifier's benches check the promise, and verification did not reach V3.
- about: operand_sampling
  text: >-
    The core samples the operand registers every clock and carries mult, shift, relu and bias with the data through
    the pipeline. An operand write during the computation may be mixed into a result in flight or ignored. The spec
    does not require it to be safe and the run did not test it.
- about: assumptions
  text: >-
    Assumptions from the interview, kept as made. The clock is the 100 MHz board oscillator, so CLKS_PER_BIT is 868.
    Weights are never -128, though the design should still compute them correctly. acc never overflows 32 bits for the
    inputs tested. Operand writes during a computation need not be safe. Shift outside 1..31 is out of contract.
    TIMEOUT_CYCLES and BUILD_STAMP defaults and the DOTQ ID presentation were defaulted by the oracle, not decided by a
    user.
